metadata.title: The House Is a Witness.
metadata.topic: How the art, sound and music of HOUSEGHOST were designed, generated and wired into Godot

beats.narration_text: Aloha, this is Liam, in for Bear. Today we take apart a game about a boy nobody is looking for. It is called HOUSEGHOST, it was built in Godot by Narasimha Reddy Valam, and the whole thing turns on one key.

beats.role_note: The premise. Real capture underneath. Author credit card appears on screen here.
beats.narration_text: A boy is missing from this house. The version everyone agreed on is that he ran away. It was easier to believe than the alternative, and nobody looked very hard. He did not run. You play him. A new family lives here now. His bedroom has been emptied and taped into boxes, and there is a clean rectangle on the wallpaper where something of his used to stand.

show.event: on-screen credit: HOUSEGHOST — Narasimha Reddy Valam

beats.role_note: The flip, live from the capture at 11.65 s. The lie and the truth.
beats.narration_text: He can still see the room the way it was, and the game lets you see it too. Press the key and the light turns warm, the bed is made, his drawings go back up on the wall. That warm room is the comfortable version. It is also the lie. The stripped one is what is actually there. The camera never rotates. What turns over is gravity, and the truth.

beats.role_note: What he wants, the girl, and the man. Storyboard panel 06 appears LABELLED as a later night — it is not in the slice.
beats.narration_text: He wants one thing. Not revenge, not escape. To be noticed by somebody, once, before the anniversary of the night he supposedly left. There is a girl of about eight in the doorway, and she is the only person in this house who might still see him. And there is a man downstairs who checks the cellar door every night, and lays a line of salt across it, for a reason nobody has asked him about.

beats.role_note: Scope honesty — this is the first night of something longer.
beats.narration_text: What follows is the first night. Three relics, seven days on the calendar, one room. The full game runs longer, the house gets less honest as it goes, and the question of who the salt is for does not get answered tonight. This is the opening of the story, built to prove the thing works. It is not the whole of it.

beats.role_note: Three pillars, each cutting to the engine moment that serves it.
beats.narration_text: Three pillars, and each one had to survive contact with a key press. The house is a witness: nothing is narrated, and his lines sit in the level, in his voice, where they mean something. Being seen costs: recognition and the calendar are the same meter filling. And nothing shown, everything implied. The man never appears. The clean rectangle on the wallpaper does. That third pillar disciplines the other two. The game does not show you the thing it is about. It shows you the shape left behind.

beats.role_note: The causal hole and the decision that closed it. Contact lands at 12.88 s in the capture.
beats.narration_text: An early version had a counter that said things of his, found, and a goal that said be seen, and nothing in between. Collecting objects does not make a person notice you. The loop ran, and it was arbitrary. What closed the gap was deciding what a relic actually is. These are the only things left in the house that still move for him. Touch one, and something moves in a room where nothing should. That is a thing a living person can notice. Her posture carries the result. She turns further toward the room with each relic, until she is facing you with her eyes wide. The meter is a child, not a number.

beats.role_note: CODE-THEN-RESULT. flip() at reading size, then the flip in the capture.
beats.narration_text: Here is the function that turns the world over. State first, signal second, sound third. That order holds everywhere in this project. Audio is a consequence, never a cause, so muting it cannot change what the game does. That is also why both mutes exist, and why the slice still reads with every sound switched off. The nights, the relic lights and the girl's posture all carry state visually. And the guard on the first line is not decoration. Hold the key down and the flipping flag refuses the second call, so one turn makes exactly one sound.

props.title: One turn, one sound.
props.code:
func flip() -> void:
	if _flipping or _meters.ended:
		return
	_flipping = true
	is_inverted = not is_inverted

	world_flipped.emit(is_inverted)
	_audio.play("flip")

notes.label: Checked by
notes.value: 12 flip calls during one turn → 1 sound

beats.role_note: Visible result of B08 — the flip those lines produce, in real play.
beats.narration_text: And there it is. One key, and the room he remembers closes over the room that is actually there. The boy gains weight and colour on the way through. Gravity has reversed; the picture has not turned at all.

beats.role_note: CODE-THEN-RESULT. One line of gravity, then the boy standing on the ceiling.
beats.narration_text: The inversion itself is one line. The up direction flips, so he falls toward the ceiling and stands on it, and every jump from then on carries him down the screen. No camera rotation, no second level, no mirrored scene. One vector.

beats.role_note: THE REQUIRED ASSET TRACE — sheet, prompt, raw output, edits, in-engine. Five steps, no gaps.
beats.narration_text: The drawings came before the generating. Six storyboard panels, a character sheet with the poses the game would actually use, a silhouette tested at the size it appears on screen, a collision shape drawn over it, and a palette checked against the room. That sheet is the specification every generated image had to meet, and several did not. Here is one asset, end to end. The sheet. The prompt, verbatim, including the magenta backdrop, because asking a model for a transparent background returns a drawn checkerboard. The raw output, untouched. The chroma key. And the result, running.

beats.role_note: The scaling failure — three wrong measures. The most specific craft moment in the film.
beats.narration_text: Getting those frames to one size failed three times. Matching height failed, because a crouch is shorter than a stand. Matching shoulder width failed, because raised arms move the shoulders. Matching head width failed on the rising pose, where the topmost pixels are not his head. They are his hands. What finally worked was body area. Every obvious measure of the same size turned out to be a property of the pose, rather than of the boy.

beats.role_note: Rejections as evidence of judgment. Thumbnails of the takes that lost.
beats.narration_text: The takes that lost are kept. One boy was turned down for carrying less detail than the sheet specifies. A storyboard panel was turned down because a lamp had drifted from the room established two panels earlier, which only becomes visible once the earlier panels exist to disagree with. And one model was dropped altogether after it kept returning a storybook schoolchild instead of this character.

beats.role_note: CODE-THEN-RESULT — the required cause-and-effect beat. The LEVELS table, then the audible difference.
beats.narration_text: A pass over the mix found that the problem was not the levels that were set. It was the ones that were never set. Three sounds, the footsteps, the ghost's drift and the fall, were missing from this table entirely, so they played at full level, while the comment directly above it claimed footsteps were deliberately quiet. Matched peaks are not matched loudness. The footstep sample is dense where the story sounds are spiky, so at equal peaks the steps sat five decibels above the flip. The loudest sound in the game was the one that fires most often, and nothing had chosen that.

props.title: The levels that were never set.
props.code:
const LEVELS := {
	"flip":     -3.0,
	"contact":  -3.0,
	"frost":    -3.0,
	"correct":  -5.0,
	"land":    -11.0,
	"jump":    -13.0,
	"fall":     -9.0,    ## a death: still the loudest thing here, deliberately
	"step":     -9.0,    ## constant, so it sits well under every story beat
	"ghoststep": -11.0,  ## quieter again; he is not meant to sound solid
}

notes.value: +5 dB louder by RMS at matched peaks

beats.role_note: Four events in real play. On-screen label: scripted-input capture.
beats.narration_text: Nine sounds carry this slice, and four of them are the spine. Turning the world over. A contact landing. A day tearing off the calendar. And falling out of the world. Each one fires from a signal the game emits after it has already changed state, and each fires once. Holding the key, or mashing it, does not stack them.

beats.role_note: The point of the silence.
beats.narration_text: The silence is deliberate. It is the only moment in the slice where the game stops making noise on purpose, because being noticed should not sound like a reward.

beats.role_note: CODE-THEN-RESULT — the Ogg loop flag and the probe output proving the importer default.
beats.narration_text: The music ships as Ogg Vorbis, and converting the files was not the whole job. Godot's Ogg importer defaults loop to false. The probe prints it. Ogg and WAV also spell looping differently, so swapping the extensions alone gives you a score that plays once and stops. Twenty-two megabytes became one point two, and the loop is set in code, because an import setting does not survive a reimport reliably.

props.title: The importer says false.

beats.role_note: What the tests cannot do. The most useful lesson in the project.
beats.narration_text: Thirteen automated checks, zero failures. They count each sound against each event, under rapid repeats and held input, and they confirm that muting changes no game state. They were also green through every real fault this game had. Green while the player could not move, because a race between two tween signals depended on frame timing the checks never exercise. Green while three sounds fired and could not be heard. Green while a clean clone printed load errors. Passing tests and a broken game are not a contradiction. They are measuring different things. Everything that mattered was found by a person playing it, with the sound on and then with all of it off, or by running the project the way a stranger receives it. Cloned fresh, from scratch.

beats.role_note: Verdict — built, limits, contributions, models, source revision. Required content.
beats.narration_text: So what is actually here. Two character states, both versions of the room, three relics, seven nights, gravity inversion, nine sound events, two music loops, separate mutes, and a girl whose posture is the recognition meter. What tonight does not do yet: the house only gets less honest in later nights, so the hallway that rearranges itself and the cellar door are drawn and not built. Three poses on the character sheet are specified and ungenerated, because the slice never calls for them. And a player who skips the opening can take a moment to work out what the game wants of them. The cues beside each relic are the answer to that, and they have not been tried on a fresh player yet.

beats.role_note: Human and AI contributions, and which model produced which asset. Required by the brief. Author named.
beats.narration_text: HOUSEGHOST is designed, built and verified by Narasimha Reddy Valam. The game is his. The story, the inversion, the seven nights, and the decision that a child's posture should carry the meter instead of a number. He generated every image, every sound effect and both music loops, judged each one against his own character sheet and storyboard, and threw out the ones that missed. He played it with the sound on, and then with all of it off, to prove it still reads. Claude Code was the tool at the keyboard. GDScript, the processing scripts, the documentation. Every design decision in this film came from him. The art came from ChatGPT's image model. The music from Suno, under non-commercial terms. The sound effects from ElevenLabs. Gemini was tried first for the character and did not make it in, and those takes are kept, because a model that was evaluated and dropped is part of the record too.

artifactLines: Narasimha Reddy Valam — design, story, every generation, every rejection, the playtest.
Claude Code — GDScript, processing scripts, documentation.
ChatGPT image model — character art, both rooms, relics, six storyboard panels.
Suno v6-mini — two music loops, non-commercial terms, attribution.
ElevenLabs Sound Effects — the event sounds.
Gemini — evaluated for the character, dropped; no output used.

beats.role_note: Your Turn — one bounded change plus a prediction. Liam signs off here.
beats.narration_text: Your turn. Please use Walker to add a relic that can only be reached by falling upward through a ceiling gap, and predict what it does to the night count before you run it. Write the prediction down first, then run it. If the calendar disagrees with you, the interesting thing is not the bug. It is the distance between what you expected and what the engine did. That has been Liam, in for Bear. Go and turn a room over.
